prompt: A client fetches several small resources from one host. Why can reusing a TCP connection reduce latency?

options.text: Later requests avoid repeating the TCP handshake.
Each request bypasses congestion control.
The server sends every response without receiving a request.
Reusing a connection eliminates network propagation delay.

explanation: A persistent connection lets the client reuse established transport state. The initial handshake still occurred, and propagation delay and congestion control remain.

prompt: Assume sequential plaintext HTTP requests, 60 ms RTT, and negligible transfer time. How many milliseconds of TCP setup does one persistent connection save over opening a fresh one for each of four requests?

options.text: 180 ms
60 ms
240 ms
120 ms

explanation: Each fresh connection adds one handshake RTT. Four separate handshakes versus one persistent handshake save three RTTs, or \(3\times60=180\) ms.

prompt: A browser opens several TCP connections to one origin to fetch page assets in parallel. What is the main trade-off?

options.text: It can overlap responses, at the cost of extra handshakes and transport state.
It eliminates transport loss, at the cost of slower DNS.
It prevents HTTP head-of-line blocking on every connection without overhead.
It forces the server to serialize all responses across those connections.

explanation: Separate connections can carry responses independently, but each has setup and congestion state. They also compete with other flows at shared bottlenecks.

prompt: Which relationship describes the three main units of HTTP/2?

options.text: A connection has streams; each message on a stream is made of one or more frames.
A frame contains several TCP connections; each one transports one message.
A stream is one frame, and a message is one connection.
Only one stream can exist per connection, regardless of the frame format.

explanation: A stream is a bidirectional logical channel. HTTP messages carry requests or responses, and frames are the smaller units used to encode them.

prompt: Which information lets an HTTP/2 endpoint tell interleaved frames for two requests apart?

options.text: The stream identifier in the frame header.
The destination IP address of each frame.
The TLS certificate serial number.
The HTTP method in every data frame.

explanation: Both requests can use the same connection and network endpoints. The stream ID identifies which logical stream a frame belongs to.

prompt: An API moves to HTTP/2. Which aspect can remain unchanged while the wire representation switches to binary frames?

options.text: The meaning of GET, status codes, and headers.
The order of every byte in the original HTTP/1.x text stream.
The rule requiring one TCP connection per resource.
The reliance on opening a separate stream for every individual frame.

explanation: HTTP/2 preserves HTTP semantics while changing encoding and multiplexing at the framing layer.

prompt: One HTTP/2 stream carries a large download and another carries a small response needed to render the page. How can multiplexing and prioritization help?

options.text: The sender can interleave frames and give the critical stream earlier service.
TCP delivers a later segment around a gap if it is from the critical stream.
The browser must finish the large download because streams cannot interleave.
Prioritization opens a separate UDP socket for each HTTP/2 request.

explanation: At the HTTP layer, interleaving prevents one whole response from needing to finish before another starts. Prioritization is a scheduling signal, while TCP still delivers a single ordered byte stream.

prompt: Two browsers load the same page but give different priority hints for the same resources. What is the likely consequence when bandwidth is limited?

options.text: The order of service and time to render can differ.
HTTP status codes have different meanings in the browsers.
Lower-priority resources are automatically dropped.
TLS chooses different cryptographic keys for each priority level.

explanation: Priority can influence scheduling under competition. Different browser policies and server implementations can therefore lead to different performance.

prompt: What saves bytes when HTTP/2 repeatedly sends the same header field values?

options.text: Header compression can refer to previously indexed fields.
TLS stops encrypting headers on reuse.
TCP acknowledges repeated fields instead of carrying them.
The HTTP/2 server discards all repeated headers.

explanation: HPACK can encode repeated fields with indexed representations maintained by both endpoints, reducing header overhead.

prompt: A TCP segment carrying HTTP/2 stream A data is lost. Later bytes containing stream B data arrive before retransmission. Why can stream B still stall?

options.text: TCP's shared ordered byte stream blocks delivery past the missing range.
HTTP/2 provides no stream identifier to distinguish the arriving frames.
HTTP/2 treats all streams as one request requiring one complete response.
TCP delivers later bytes immediately but HTTP/2 forbids concurrent responses.

explanation: The transport withholds bytes behind the missing segment. HTTP/2 removes response-order coupling at its own layer but cannot bypass TCP’s in-order delivery.

prompt: Which stack correctly places HTTP/3 above its underlying protocols, from highest to lowest here?

options.text: HTTP/3 → QUIC → UDP → IP
HTTP/3 → UDP → QUIC → IP
HTTP/3 → TLS → TCP → IP
QUIC → HTTP/3 → TCP → IP

explanation: HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams. QUIC runs over UDP datagrams and integrates its TLS 1.3 handshake.

prompt: Two independent HTTP/3 streams use one QUIC connection. A packet carrying only stream A data is lost. Select two correct statements.

options.text: Already received data on stream B can be delivered without waiting for A’s retransmission.
Congestion control can still reduce the shared sending rate after the loss.
QUIC must withhold all stream B deliveries until stream A is complete.
QUIC does not retransmit reliable stream data because it uses UDP.

explanation: In-order delivery is enforced per stream, so missing bytes in A do not create a delivery gap in B. The streams still share congestion control and available connection capacity.

prompt: Why does using UDP under QUIC not imply that QUIC sends without congestion control?

options.text: QUIC implements congestion control itself above UDP.
UDP implements TCP-style congestion windows by default.
HTTP headers specify how many UDP packets the routers may forward.
QUIC leaves rate control entirely to the receiving application.

explanation: UDP provides datagrams. QUIC implements transport functions such as congestion control, acknowledgments, and recovery.

prompt: When can QUIC use TLS 0-RTT to send application data in the first flight?

options.text: On resumption with suitable prior state and server acceptance of early data
On first contact without any previously established server-related state
After a separate TCP handshake has established a connection to the server
After congestion control has observed a round trip without any packet loss

explanation: 0-RTT is conditional on resumption state and early-data policy. It is not the normal handshake guarantee for a new peer, and early data can face replay constraints.

prompt: Which statement best compares handshake latency for a fresh QUIC connection and a resumed connection that accepts 0-RTT data?

options.text: Fresh setup uses a handshake RTT; resumption can send early data in its first flight.
Fresh setup sends no handshake; resumption must complete one before sending data.
Both require a TCP handshake before either can exchange their TLS messages.
Both send ordinary application data immediately without prior server state.

explanation: QUIC integrates transport establishment and TLS. The 0-RTT option removes a setup wait for eligible early data, but its response still must travel across the network.

prompt: Why can distinct QUIC packet numbers help a sender obtain more precise RTT samples after retransmission?

options.text: The ACK identifies which packet transmission arrived, avoiding retransmission ambiguity.
The ACK reuses the original packet number, assigning both transmissions one timestamp.
The application adds an RTT measurement to every ACK before QUIC processes it.
The connection ID contains an RTT sample that is updated by every forwarding router.

explanation: QUIC retransmits lost information in a newly numbered packet. The ACK can identify which packet actually arrived, reducing the ambiguity caused by reused transmission identifiers.
